Target the strongest likely original or authoritative source for each angle, then drill into specifics once the map is laid out.
- PREFER PRIMARY AND AUTHORITATIVE SOURCES: original announcements, filings, specifications, measurements, peer-reviewed work, official documentation — over aggregator summaries and secondhand commentary. Start this on the first turn: do not spend the opening source budget on generic latest/best/breakthrough roundup queries. If a generic search is needed to discover names, use its very next query to find the original.
- CHASE CITATIONS UPSTREAM. If a page reports a named study, benchmark, filing, announcement, or dataset, keep that original work as an open lead until you find it or have genuinely exhausted targeted searches. Use the original for the finding; retain the summary only when it adds distinct interpretation.
- TREAT WEAK SECONDARY PAGES AS LEADS, NOT PROOF. Do not mark a load-bearing angle covered when its evidence is only listicles, consultancy or vendor marketing, prediction pages, or anonymous summaries. Keep the angle open and pivot with a targeted site: query to the named institution, paper, regulator, filing, model card, specification, or strong independent reporting. Multiple pages from one domain are one source, not independent corroboration.

Security evaluations at both user-study and large-scale model-testing scale find that AI assistance increases insecure code and that nearly half of AI-generated code samples introduce vulnerabilities, with trust in AI output falling even as usage rises [[66ce65_p1]] [[834012_p0]] [[61d060_p0]].

Reliability assessment is constrained by benchmark design, where the most cited measure of real-world issue resolution, SWE-bench Verified, relies on existing repository tests that can accept plausible but incorrect patches, and where independent re-evaluation has documented meaningful false-positive rates [[05b864_p0]] [[85fbf9_p0]]. The decisive uncertainty is not whether agents can generate functional code quickly in isolated tasks, but whether organizations can absorb the review, testing, and maintenance burden required to make that code safe and maintainable at scale [[020419_p1]] [[66ce65_p1]] [[85fbf9_p0]].

## Productivity: from lab acceleration to field stagnation

The earliest quantitative claim for AI coding assistance comes from a GitHub-led randomized experiment with 95 professional developers, where the group using GitHub Copilot completed an identical programming task in an average of 1 hour 11 minutes versus 2 hours 41 minutes for the control group, a 55% faster completion rate with statistical significance at P=.0017 and a 95% confidence interval of 21% to 89% [[150f02_p4]] [[5c047a_p0]]. | METR early-2025 | 16 experienced OSS developers, 246 real issues in own repos | Measured completion time | 19% slower with AI, yet 20% faster perceived | [[91fbd2_p0]] |

Taken together, the evidence suggests that speed gains are most robust in short, well-specified, repetitive tasks in controlled environments, while complex, repository-specific work with experienced developers shows no gain or a net slowdown once review and debugging are included [[150f02_p4]] [[91fbd2_p0]] [[01298f_p1]]. The convergence between METR and Uplevel on the gap between perception and measurement, and between DORA 2024 and Uplevel on the lack of delivery-level improvement, contrasts with the convergence between GitHub's lab result and DORA 2025's self-reported productivity gains, highlighting that self-report and satisfaction do not reliably predict throughput [[91fbd2_p0]] [[bfbda7_p0]] [[b67f42_p2]]. For engineering leaders, the practical implication is that productivity should be assessed at the delivery system level, not the individual suggestion level, and that gains in documentation quality and review speed do not automatically translate into faster, more stable releases [[1253eb_p1]] [[1253eb_p0]].

The divergence also reflects differences in what is being measured, as GitHub's lab task isolates coding time on a greenfield-style problem, while METR and Uplevel capture the full cycle of understanding context, integrating changes, and fixing introduced defects in existing codebases [[150f02_p4]] [[91fbd2_p0]] [[bfbda7_p0]]. DORA's finding that AI adoption is associated with higher code review speed but lower delivery stability suggests that faster generation can create a bottleneck downstream if review capacity and test coverage do not scale accordingly [[1253eb_p0]] [[1253eb_p1]]. This helps explain why developers can feel more productive and satisfied while delivery metrics remain flat, as the cognitive relief of offloading boilerplate is real but does not necessarily reduce the total work required to ship safe, maintainable code [[150f02_p3]] [[150f02_p5]] [[01298f_p1]].

## Reliability and correctness: what benchmarks measure and miss

SWE-bench has become the primary measure of whether a coding agent can do real engineering work, by tasking models to resolve real GitHub issues across 12 popular Python repositories and verifying patches against existing test suites [[32f395_p0]] [[68e580_p0]]. The benchmark requires understanding and coordinating changes across multiple functions, classes, and files, interacting with execution environments, and processing long contexts [[0f13e9_p1]]. Because the original dataset contains noisy and underspecified instances, OpenAI and Princeton curated SWE-bench Verified, a human-validated subset of 500 instances where annotators reviewed problem descriptions, test patches, and solvability [[05b864_p0]] [[ac1d47_p0]]. Even this curated subset is evaluated by applying the test patch and generated patch to the buggy repository and checking whether modified test files pass, a validation process that is intentionally narrow [[85fbf9_p1]].

The limitation of that validation is central to reliability claims, as testing is rarely exhaustive and a patch may pass the relevant tests while failing to match developer expectations [[85fbf9_p0]] [[0c8636_p0]]. An empirical study of plausible patches on SWE-bench Verified introduced a differential patch testing technique, PatchDiff, to generate tests that reveal behavioral differences between generated and human-written ground-truth patches, finding that evaluations suffer from plausible but incorrect patches that inflate resolution rates [[85fbf9_p0]] [[0c8636_p0]]. A separate investigation of test overfitting on SWE-bench found that LLM-generated code patches can overfit to auto-generated reproduction tests, and that refining code to pass observed tests can break other functionality, with mitigation attempts reducing both overfitting and overall effectiveness [[b4c964_p0]] [[b4c964_p2]]. The evidence suggests that passing the benchmark's tests is a necessary but not sufficient condition for correctness, and that reported pass rates should be interpreted as an upper bound on true issue resolution [[85fbf9_p0]] [[b4c964_p2]].
